title: Ordinary weak uniformization with an integral proper covering witness
statement: Let $Y$ be a nonempty integral Noetherian scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme], where Noetherian means a finite affine cover by spectra of Noetherian rings [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Assume it has an affine open cover whose coordinate rings are quasi-excellent [def-exc-excellent-ring]. There are finitely many nonempty integral regular Noetherian schemes $T_i$ [def-weil-regular-scheme] and dominant generically finite finite-type morphisms $f_i:T_i\to Y$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], an integral Noetherian scheme $P$, a proper surjective generically finite morphism $g:P\to Y$ [def-weil-proper-morphism] [def-weil-surjective-morphism], an open cover $P=\bigcup_iP_i$ [def-weil-open-immersion], and $Y$-morphisms $P_i\to T_i$. Dominant means dense image; generically finite means that the induced extension of function fields is finite, where the function field is the local ring at the generic point. No invertibility or prime-to-a-prime degree condition is imposed.

source.place: Expose VII Theorem 1.1, printed p.81, with empty boundary, and Expose II Theorem 3.2.1, the ordinary-alteration case (parameter 1), printed p.29. The latter gives an integral proper-surjective witness and Zariski opens refining the given regular alteration cover. This ordinary case is not the prime-to-a-prime version; no Stacks tag gives this combined theorem.

proof.text: Use the ordinary topology and marked predicate $U(S,Z)$ of [def-per-ordinary-alteration-topology]. We prove $U$ for all reduced quasi-excellent Noetherian schemes by induction on a finite dimension bound, and then use the unbounded reduction. This retains boundary data during the induction even though the item will use $Z=\varnothing$. The complete-local reduction applies with no invertible prime.

For a normal complete local domain $A$ of dimension zero, the only prime is $(0)$, so every nonzero element is a unit: $A$ is a field. Its spectrum is regular and its only nowhere dense closed subset is empty. In dimension one, [lem-sc-normal-dim1-dvr] makes $A$ a DVR. Its maximal ideal is generated by a uniformizer; its only other prime is $(0)$, whose localization is a field. Thus its spectrum is regular by [def-weil-regular-scheme]. A nowhere dense closed subset is empty or the closed point, the latter cut out by the uniformizer. It is a strict normal crossings boundary with one regular zero-dimensional component and codimension one. The identity cover gives $U$ in both dimensions.

Let $d\ge2$ and suppose $U$ is known for all reduced quasi-excellent Noetherian schemes of dimension at most $d-1$. For $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ normal complete local of dimension $d$ and nowhere dense $Z$, apply [lem-per-complete-local-nodal-dimension-reduction]. It gives a finite ordinary covering $M_a\to X$ by integral excellent Noetherian log regular pairs $(M_a,B_a)$, with the inverse image of $Z$ cut out by an effective Cartier ideal and contained in $B_a$. These are precisely the hypotheses needed for log resolution; no regularity has yet been claimed.

Apply [lem-per-noetherian-log-pair-strict-resolution] to each $(M_a,B_a)$. Obtain integral regular Noetherian $R_a$, proper birational $e_a:R_a\to M_a$, and a strict normal crossings boundary $A_a$ containing $e_a^{-1}(B_a)$. These maps are ordinary singleton alteration covers: proper birational means finite type, surjective (its closed image contains a dense open), and function-field degree one. Finite-type composition puts $R_a\to X$ in $\operatorname{alt}/X$; the function-field extensions compose. The covering-sieve transitivity axiom composes these singleton covers with the finite covering $(M_a\to X)_a$.

The Cartier ideal on $M_a$ remains Cartier on $R_a$: a local nonzero generator stays nonzero under the dominant map between integral schemes, hence is a non-zero-divisor. At a point of $R_a$, take the boundary parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ supplied by log resolution, and a generator $f$ of that pullback ideal. Since $V(f)\subseteq V(t_1\cdots t_r)$, some power of $t_1\cdots t_r$ belongs to $(f)$, so $f$ becomes a unit after their product is inverted. The boundary factorization lemma gives $f=u\prod t_i^{a_i}$. Its reduced zero-set is therefore the union of exactly the coordinate divisors with $a_i>0$. Globally these are a subset of the finitely many components of $A_a$, so their reduced union is a strict normal crossings boundary by the regular-intersection definition. It has support exactly the inverse image of $Z$. Thus the composite covering gives $U(X,Z)$.

source.place: VII 4.2--4.3, pp.82--83; boundary monomial argument made explicit

proof.text: The bounded local-reduction theorem now gives $U$ for every reduced quasi-excellent Noetherian scheme of dimension at most $d$. Starting with the dimension-zero and dimension-one cases and repeating Steps 3--5 proves the complete-local hypothesis in every finite dimension. The unbounded clause of the same theorem gives $U$ for arbitrary reduced quasi-excellent Noetherian schemes, without a global dimension bound.

Apply $U$ to the given integral $Y$ and $Z=\varnothing$. Obtain a finite ordinary alteration covering $(T_b\to Y)_b$ with nonempty integral regular Noetherian sources. An object of $\operatorname{alt}/Y$ is finite type and takes the unique generic point to that of $Y$, with finite residue-field extension. Thus each map is dominant and generically finite in exactly the sense of the item.

source.place: VII Theorem 1.1 with empty boundary, p.81

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-ordinary-alteration-proper-refinement] to this covering of $Y$. Obtain integral Noetherian $P$, proper surjective generically finite $g:P\to Y$, and finitely many opens $P_j$ covering $P$ with maps $P_j\to T_{b(j)}$. Reindex the regular schemes by $j$, allowing repeated copies of a $T_b$; discard any empty $P_j$. This gives the common index set required in the statement and all of its factorization triangles. None of these steps selects a prime or places a degree restriction on the function fields.

proof_origin.place: VII 2.1--4.3, pp.81--83, induction with marked boundaries; III 6.2, pp.43--45; II 3.2.1, ordinary case, p.29. Boundary sub-divisor calculation expanded explicitly.
